guide_line: Name the cation, then the anion. Use a Roman numeral for a variable metal charge, and use prefixes only for two nonmetals.
steps: Ionic names start with the cation and end with the anion. Group 1, group 2, aluminum, zinc, silver, and cadmium have fixed charges, so they get no Roman numeral and no prefix.
Iron, copper, tin, lead, chromium, cobalt, and mercury need a Roman numeral for the cation charge. The numeral is the charge, not the subscript. FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride.

A monatomic anion uses a stem plus -ide: chloride, oxide, sulfide, nitride, phosphide. Polyatomic ions keep their own names: nitrate, nitrite, sulfate, sulfite, phosphate, hydroxide, carbonate, hydrogen carbonate, ammonium, acetate, cyanide, chromate, dichromate, perchlorate, chlorate, chlorite, hypochlorite.
If the formula starts with a metal or with ammonium, name it as ionic and skip prefixes. If it is only nonmetals, use prefixes. NO2 is nitrogen dioxide. NaNO2 is sodium nitrite.
Parentheses group a polyatomic ion. They do not appear in the name. Mg(NO3)2 is magnesium nitrate.
O2− is oxide, as in Na2O. O2^2− is peroxide, as in Na2O2, sodium peroxide. The mercury(I) ion is Hg2^2+, so mercury(I) chloride is Hg2Cl2.

Two nonmetals use prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa, hepta, octa, nona, deca. Skip mono on the first element only. Drop the last a or o of a prefix before oxide: monoxide, tetroxide, pentoxide.
An acid with H and one other nonmetal is hydro + stem + ic acid. HCl gas is hydrogen chloride. HCl in water is hydrochloric acid.
For an oxyacid, -ate becomes -ic acid and -ite becomes -ous acid. H2SO4 is sulfuric acid, H2SO3 is sulfurous acid, HNO3 is nitric acid, and HNO2 is nitrous acid.
A hydrate is the salt name plus a prefix and hydrate. MgSO4·7H2O is magnesium sulfate heptahydrate.
Iron is a metal and chlorine is a nonmetal, so the compound is ionic. Do not use a prefix.
Each chloride is 1−. Two chlorides mean the iron ion is 2+.

similar_problem.hint: Three chloride ions total 3−. The iron charge that balances them is written as a Roman numeral, not as the prefix tri.

problems.why: Each Cl is 1− and there are three, so iron is 3+. FeCl3 is ionic, and the name is iron(III) chloride.
hints: Three chloride ions total 3−. The iron charge that balances them is written as a Roman numeral, not as the prefix tri.

problems.why: Magnesium is always 2+, so no Roman numeral is used. Ionic names do not use the prefix di. MgCl2 is magnesium chloride.
hints: Magnesium’s charge never changes. Leave out both a Roman numeral and the prefix di.

problems.why: Mg2+ and O2− make an ionic compound of a fixed-charge metal. The name is magnesium oxide.
hints: Both ions in MgO have charge size 2, and magnesium does not need a numeral. End the nonmetal in -ide.

problems.why: NO3− is nitrate. Magnesium is 2+, so two nitrate ions appear in the formula. The name does not say di. Mg(NO3)2 is magnesium nitrate.
hints: NO3− is named nitrate. The 2 outside the parentheses is already fixed by magnesium’s charge, so it stays out of the name.

problems.why: Oxide is 2−. Two copper ions share that charge, so each copper is 1+. Cu2O is copper(I) oxide.
hints: One oxide ion is 2−. Split that charge across the two copper ions before you pick the Roman numeral.

problems.why: One oxide is 2−, and there is one copper ion, so copper is 2+. CuO is copper(II) oxide.
hints: This formula has one copper and one oxide. Oxide is 2−, so the copper numeral is not I.

problems.why: N2O4 is two nonmetals, so prefixes are required. Two nitrogens give di, and four oxygens give tetra. The a in tetra drops before oxide: dinitrogen tetroxide.
hints: Count two nitrogens and four oxygens. Drop the a at the end of tetra when the next word is oxide.

problems.why: CO has one carbon and one oxygen. Mono is left off the first element and kept on the second. Mono plus oxide is written monoxide: carbon monoxide.
hints: There is one carbon, so the first name gets no prefix. Keep mono on oxygen and blend it into monoxide.

problems.why: Two nitrogen atoms need the prefix di. One oxygen keeps mono, written as monoxide. N2O is dinitrogen monoxide.
hints: The subscript is on nitrogen, not on oxygen. Oxygen’s prefix is mono, written as monoxide.

problems.why: Sulfur and fluorine are nonmetals. One sulfur has no prefix. Six fluorines use hexa, and the anion-style ending is -ide: sulfur hexafluoride.
hints: One sulfur gets no prefix. The prefix for six goes on fluorine, and the ending is -ide.

problems.why: PCl5 is molecular. The element name is phosphorus, not phosphorous. Five chlorines use penta: phosphorus pentachloride.
hints: Spell the element phosphorus with -us. Five chlorines use penta, and this is not an ionic Roman-numeral name.

problems.why: H2SO4 comes from sulfate. An -ate ion becomes an -ic acid, with no hydro prefix. The name is sulfuric acid.
hints: H2SO4 comes from sulfate, an -ate ion. Change -ate to -ic acid and do not add hydro.

problems.why: HNO2 comes from nitrite. An -ite ion becomes an -ous acid. The name is nitrous acid.
hints: NO2− is nitrite, the -ite ion. An -ite oxyacid ends in -ous, not -ic.

problems.q: Name HCl dissolved in water, as an acid.
problems.why: Aqueous HCl is a binary acid. The name uses hydro, the stem of chlorine, and ic acid: hydrochloric acid.
hints: This HCl is in water and has only two elements. Binary acids start with hydro and end with ic acid.

problems.q: Name HCl as a gas, not as an acid.
problems.why: Gaseous HCl is named as a molecular compound: hydrogen chloride. Hydrochloric acid is the name of the water solution.
hints: The gas is not the acid name. Name hydrogen first, then the nonmetal stem with -ide.

problems.why: The mercury(I) cation is the diatomic ion Hg2^2+. Two chloride ions balance it, giving Hg2Cl2. Each mercury is counted as 1+, so the Stock name is mercury(I) chloride.
hints: The cation in this salt is Hg2^2+, not a single Hg2+ ion. The Roman numeral on mercury is I.

problems.why: Na2O2 contains the peroxide ion O2^2−, not oxide. The name is sodium peroxide. Sodium oxide would be Na2O.
hints: Na2O would be the oxide. The O2 group in Na2O2 is the peroxide ion, so use that name.

problems.why: Each sulfate is 2− and there are three, for a total of 6−. Two chromium ions share that charge, so each is 3+. The name is chromium(III) sulfate.
hints: Three sulfate ions are 6− altogether. Divide that charge by the two chromium ions to get the numeral.

problems.q: Write the formula of iron(III) oxide.
problems.why: Iron(III) is Fe3+ and oxide is O2−. Crossing the charges gives two irons and three oxides: Fe2O3.
hints: Iron(III) is 3+ and oxide is 2−. Cross those two numbers to place the subscripts.

problems.q: Write the formula of calcium phosphate.
problems.why: Calcium is Ca2+ and phosphate is PO4^3−. Three calcium ions and two phosphate ions balance. Phosphate stays in parentheses: Ca3(PO4)2.
hints: Calcium is 2+ and phosphate is 3−. Keep PO4 inside parentheses because more than one phosphate is required.

problems.q: Write the formula of ammonium sulfate.
problems.why: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfate is SO4^2−. Two ammonium ions balance one sulfate. The formula is (NH4)2SO4.
hints: Ammonium is NH4+ and sulfate is 2−. Put parentheses around NH4 because the subscript is greater than 1.

problems.q: Write the formula of magnesium sulfate heptahydrate.
problems.why: Magnesium sulfate is MgSO4. Hepta means seven waters. The hydrate formula is MgSO4·7H2O.
hints: Hepta means seven. Write the salt MgSO4, then a dot and seven H2O units.

problems.q: Write the formula of sulfurous acid.
problems.why: Sulfurous acid comes from sulfite, SO3^2−. Two H+ ions balance that charge. The formula is H2SO3.
hints: Sulfurous comes from sulfite, not sulfate. Sulfite is SO3^2−, and the acid needs two hydrogens.

problems.q: Write the formula of copper(II) nitrate.
problems.why: Copper(II) is Cu2+ and nitrate is NO3−. Two nitrates balance one copper(II) ion: Cu(NO3)2.
hints: Copper(II) is 2+ and each nitrate is 1−. More than one nitrate means parentheses around NO3.

problems.why: ClO− is hypochlorite. The hypo- prefix stays, and -ite becomes -ous acid. HClO is hypochlorous acid.
hints: ClO− is hypochlorite. Keep hypo, and turn the -ite ending into -ous acid.

problems.q: Write the formula of perchloric acid.
problems.why: Perchloric acid comes from perchlorate, ClO4−. One hydrogen balances the 1− charge. The formula is HClO4.
hints: Perchloric acid comes from perchlorate. That ion has four oxygens and a 1− charge.

problems.why: Na+ and Cl− are fixed-charge ions. No numeral and no prefix are used. NaCl is sodium chloride.
hints: Sodium’s charge is always 1+. Change the halogen ending to -ide and add nothing else.

problems.why: Silver is treated as Ag+ in this naming system, so no Roman numeral is written. NO3− is nitrate. AgNO3 is silver nitrate.
hints: Silver is one of the fixed-charge metals in this chapter, so skip the numeral. NO3− is nitrate.

problems.why: Zinc is always Zn2+. The compound is ionic, so the subscript 2 does not become the prefix di. ZnCl2 is zinc chloride.
hints: Zinc’s charge is fixed at 2+. An ionic name does not turn the subscript 2 into di.

problems.why: NH4+ is ammonium and CO3^2− is carbonate. The name is ammonium carbonate.
hints: NH4+ is ammonium and CO3^2− is carbonate. Do not invent prefixes for either ion.

problems.why: Aluminum is always Al3+, so no Roman numeral is used. SO4^2− is sulfate. Al2(SO4)3 is aluminum sulfate.
hints: Aluminum’s charge is always 3+, so no numeral is needed. SO4^2− is sulfate, and the subscripts stay out of the name.

problems.q: Use Fe = 55.845 and O = 15.9994. What is the molar mass of Fe2O3, in g/mol, to 4 significant figures?
problems.why: 2(55.845) + 3(15.9994) = 111.690 + 47.9982 = 159.6882. To 4 significant figures, the molar mass is 159.7 g/mol.
hints: Iron(III) oxide has two Fe atoms and three O atoms. Add those five masses, then round once at the end.

problems.why: Sodium is Na+ and CN− is cyanide. The charges match, and sodium needs no Roman numeral. NaCN is sodium cyanide.
hints: CN− keeps the name cyanide. Sodium’s charge is fixed, so add no numeral and no prefix.

problems.why: K+ is potassium and OH− is hydroxide. KOH is potassium hydroxide.
hints: OH− is hydroxide. Potassium is a group 1 metal, so the name has no Roman numeral.

problems.why: The formula starts with sodium, a metal, so it is ionic. NO2− is nitrite. NaNO2 is sodium nitrite.
hints: NO2− is nitrite, one oxygen fewer than nitrate. The metal at the front means you do not write di.

problems.why: SO3^2− is sulfite. Two K+ ions balance it. Potassium has a fixed charge, so K2SO3 is potassium sulfite.
hints: SO3^2− is sulfite, not sulfate. The subscript on potassium stays out of an ionic name.

problems.why: HCO3− is hydrogen carbonate. With Na+, the name is sodium hydrogen carbonate.
hints: HCO3− is hydrogen carbonate. Sodium stays first, and the hydrogen belongs in the anion name.

problems.why: CrO4^2− is chromate. Two potassium ions balance the 2− charge. K2CrO4 is potassium chromate.
hints: CrO4^2− is chromate. Two potassium ions balance the charge, but di is not part of this name.

problems.why: Cr2O7^2− is the dichromate ion. Two sodium ions balance it. Na2Cr2O7 is sodium dichromate.
hints: Cr2O7^2− is one ion named dichromate. The di is already inside that ion name, not a prefix on sodium.

problems.why: CH3COO− is acetate. Paired with Na+, the name is sodium acetate.
hints: CH3COO− is acetate. The carbons and hydrogens stay inside that ion’s name.

problems.q: Write the formula of calcium hydroxide.
problems.why: Calcium is Ca2+ and hydroxide is OH−. Two hydroxide ions balance one calcium ion. The formula is Ca(OH)2.
hints: Calcium is 2+ and each hydroxide is 1−. Put parentheses around OH before the subscript 2.

problems.q: Write the formula of aluminum hydroxide.
problems.why: Aluminum is Al3+ and hydroxide is OH−. Three hydroxide ions balance one aluminum ion. The formula is Al(OH)3.
hints: Aluminum is 3+ and each hydroxide is 1−. Parentheses go around OH, then the subscript is 3.

problems.q: Write the formula of potassium cyanide.
problems.why: Potassium is K+ and cyanide is CN−. The charges already match, so the formula is KCN.
hints: Potassium is 1+ and cyanide is 1−. Both subscripts stay 1, so neither number is written.

problems.q: Write the formula of sodium sulfite.
problems.why: Sulfite is SO3^2−. Two Na+ ions balance that charge. The formula is Na2SO3.
hints: Sulfite is SO3^2−, one oxygen fewer than sulfate. Two sodium ions balance the 2− charge.

problems.why: CO2 is two nonmetals, so prefixes are required. One carbon gets no mono. Two oxygens make dioxide. The name is carbon dioxide.
hints: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals. Leave the first element unnumbered, and use di for two oxygens.

problems.why: NO2 has no metal, so it is molecular. One nitrogen is named without mono, and two oxygens need di. The name is nitrogen dioxide.
hints: There is no metal in NO2, so this is not nitrite. Two oxygen atoms need the prefix di.

problems.why: Two nitrogen atoms need di. Five oxygen atoms need penta, and the final a drops before oxide. N2O5 is dinitrogen pentoxide.
hints: Count two nitrogens and five oxygens. Drop the final a of penta when the next word is oxide.

problems.why: HNO3 comes from nitrate. The -ate ending becomes -ic acid, and an oxyacid does not use hydro. The name is nitric acid.
hints: Nitrate ends in -ate, so the acid ends in -ic. Leave hydro off an acid that contains oxygen.

problems.why: H3PO4 comes from phosphate. The -ate ending becomes -ic acid. The name is phosphoric acid.
hints: Phosphate ends in -ate, so this oxyacid ends in -ic. Spell the stem phosphoric.

problems.why: Tin is a metal with more than one charge, and four chloride ions total 4−. The tin charge is 4+. SnCl4 is tin(IV) chloride.
hints: Four chloride ions total 4−. Tin’s charge is the Roman numeral, and tetra is the wrong tool here.

problems.why: Sulfate is SO4^2−, so the iron ion is Fe2+. FeSO4 is iron(II) sulfate.
hints: Sulfate is 2−. The iron charge that balances one sulfate ion is written as a Roman numeral.

problems.why: NH4+ is ammonium and Cl− is chloride. NH4Cl is ammonium chloride.
hints: NH4+ is ammonium and Cl− is chloride. Neither ion takes a Greek prefix.

problems.why: Barium is always Ba2+, so no Roman numeral is used. NO3− is nitrate. Ba(NO3)2 is barium nitrate.
hints: Barium’s charge is fixed at 2+. The parentheses only show two nitrate ions, and they stay out of the name.

problems.q: Write the formula of ammonium nitrate.
problems.why: Ammonium is NH4+ and nitrate is NO3−. One of each ion balances. The formula is NH4NO3.
hints: Ammonium is 1+ and nitrate is 1−. One of each ion already balances, so no extra subscript is written.

problems.why: ClO3− is chlorate. With K+, the name is potassium chlorate.
hints: ClO3− is chlorate, the -ate ion with three oxygens. Potassium needs no numeral.

problems.why: ClO2− is chlorite, one oxygen fewer than chlorate. KClO2 is potassium chlorite.
hints: Two oxygens on chlorine make the -ite ion, chlorite. Do not drop down to hypo or up to chlorate.

problems.why: ClO− is hypochlorite. KClO is potassium hypochlorite.
hints: One oxygen on chlorine is the hypo…ite ion. Attach that anion name after potassium.

problems.why: ClO4− is perchlorate, one oxygen more than chlorate. KClO4 is potassium perchlorate.
hints: Four oxygens on chlorine add the prefix per to chlorate. The metal name stays potassium.

problems.why: Sulfur and chlorine are both nonmetals, so prefixes are required. One sulfur gets no mono, and two chlorines need di. SCl2 is sulfur dichloride.
hints: Sulfur and chlorine are both nonmetals. Two chlorines need di, and the first element stays singular.
